questions.stem: Commonest complication of Mumps is:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Encephalitis: Incorrect. Mumps encephalitis is a possible but less common complication (occurring in about 0.1-0.2% of cases). While mumps can cause viral meningitis (which is more common than encephalitis), the severe inflammation of brain tissue leading to encephalitis is rare compared to orchitis and oophoritis. (C) Pneumonia: Incorrect. Mumps virus primarily affects the salivary glands, testes, and central nervous system, but it does not typically cause pneumonia. Lower respiratory tract involvement is very rare, and when present, it is usually mild and self-limiting. Other respiratory viruses, such as influenza or RSV, are far more commonly associated with pneumonia. (D) Myocarditis: Incorrect. Mumps-associated myocarditis is extremely rare and occurs in very few cases. While viral myocarditis can be caused by many different viruses (e.g., Coxsackievirus B), mumps virus is not a common cause. It is considered an exceptional complication rather than the most common one.

questions.stem: Regarding mumps, which is true?

options.label: B
options.text: Mumps causes aseptic meningitis in children

questions.answerText: Mumps causes aseptic meningitis in children
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Causes SSPE (Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis): Incorrect. SSPE is a late complication of measles virus infection, not mumps. It occurs years after an initial measles infection, leading to progressive neurological deterioration. Mumps virus does not cause SSPE. (C) Sublingual gland is involved commonly: Incorrect. Mumps primarily affects the parotid glands, leading to painful parotitis, which is the hallmark of the disease. While the submandibular and sublingual glands can be involved in some cases, parotid gland involvement is far more common. Therefore, this statement is incorrect. (D) All: Incorrect. Since options A and C are incorrect, option D cannot be the correct answer.

questions.stem: Vaccination causing intussusception:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Parvovirus: Incorrect. Parvovirus B19, which causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), is not associated with intussusception. It primarily affects red blood cell precursors, leading to aplastic crisis in individuals with hemolytic disorders (e.g., sickle cell disease), but it does not have any known link to intussusception. Additionally, no vaccine exists for Parvovirus B19. (C) Inactivated Polio Vaccine (IPV): Incorrect. Polio vaccines (both oral and inactivated) are not associated with intussusception. The oral polio vaccine (OPV) has been linked to vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) in rare cases, but neither OPV nor IPV has been associated with intussusception. (D) Measles: Incorrect. The measles vaccine, commonly given as part of the MMR (Measles, Mumps, and Rubella) vaccine, is not linked to intussusception. While the MMR vaccine can cause mild gastrointestinal symptoms, it has no established association with bowel obstruction or intussusception

questions.stem: Reassortment is typically seen in:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Herpesvirus: Incorrect. Herpesviruses, including Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), belong to the Herpesviridae family and possess a linear, double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) genome. They do not have segmented genomes, meaning reassortment cannot occur. Instead, herpesviruses primarily evolve through recombination and mutations rather than reassortment. (B) Hepadnavirus: Incorrect. Hepadnaviruses, such as Hepatitis B virus (HBV), have a partially double-stranded DNA genome that replicates via reverse transcription. Since their genome is not segmented, reassortment is not a mechanism of genetic variation in these viruses. Instead, HBV evolves through mutations and recombination. (D) Astrovirus: Incorrect. Astroviruses are non-enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) viruses. Like other non-segmented RNA viruses, they lack the ability to undergo reassortment. Instead, they evolve primarily through point mutations and recombination.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old girl has been admitted to the hospital with provisional diagnosis of rabies. The most suitable clinical sample that can confirm the antemortem diagnosis is:

options.label: B
options.text: skin impression smear for immuno-fluorescence stain

options.label: D
options.text: Giemsa stain on smear prepared from salivary secre¬tions

questions.answerText: skin impression smear for immuno-fluorescence stain
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Serum for antivirus IgG antibody: Incorrect. Serum antibody detection is not a reliable antemortem diagnostic tool because rabies virus suppresses the immune response, and antibodies typically appear late in the disease or after vaccination. Furthermore, detecting IgG alone cannot confirm active rabies infection, as it may indicate prior vaccination or exposure without disease. (C) CSF sample for viral culture: Incorrect. Rabies virus is rarely isolated from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and viral culture is neither sensitive nor practical for antemortem diagnosis. CSF analysis may show nonspecific findings like mild pleocytosis and elevated protein, but it is not definitive for rabies diagnosis. (D) Giemsa stain on smear prepared from salivary secretions: Incorrect. Although rabies virus can be present in saliva, Giemsa staining is not a suitable method for detection. Rabies virus is best detected in saliva by RT-PCR, not by Giemsa staining. Additionally, viral shedding in saliva is intermittent, making saliva testing unreliable as a sole diagnostic method.

questions.stem: A boy got unprovoked bite from a neighbor’s dog. The animal control authority caught the dog and it was found to be healthy. What will be the next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Test antibody level in the dog

options.label: B
options.text: Withhold immunization and observe the dog for 10 days for signs of rabies

questions.solutionHtml: on of Incorrect Options: (A) Test antibody level in the dog: Incorrect. Testing antibody levels in the dog is not a reliable method to determine whether the dog has rabies. Rabies diagnosis in animals is made through direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing on brain tissue post-mortem, not by checking antibodies. Serologic testing does not confirm active rabies infection, as vaccinated animals may have antibodies without being infected. (B) Withhold immunization and observe the dog for 10 days for signs of rabies: Incorrect. While 10-day observation is recommended for the dog, it should not delay starting PEP in the bitten individual, especially for an unprovoked bite. If the dog develops signs of rabies within the 10-day observation period, it confirms the risk of transmission, making early PEP critical. Delaying treatment could lead to a fatal outcome if the virus has already entered the nervous system. (D) Perform euthanasia for the dog: Incorrect. Euthanasia is not necessary for a healthy dog simply because it bit someone. Instead, the dog should be observed for 10 days for any signs of rabies. If the dog remains healthy, it was likely not infectious at the time of the bite, and PEP can be stopped if already started. However, if the dog shows signs of rabies, it should be euthanized and tested immediately.

questions.stem: Diagnostic of Rabies:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Guarneri bodies: Incorrect. Guarneri bodies are intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies found in epithelial cells in smallpox (Variola virus) and cowpox infections. They are not associated with rabies and are primarily seen in skin lesions of poxvirus infections. (C) Cowdry A bodies: Incorrect. Cowdry A bodies are intranuclear eosinophilic inclusion bodies found in herpesvirus infections, particularly herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV). They are not associated with rabies, as rabies virus is an RNA virus that forms cytoplasmic inclusions, not nuclear inclusions. (D) Bollinger bodies: Incorrect. Bollinger bodies are large intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies found in fowlpox virus infections (a type of avian poxvirus). These are specific to birds and have no relevance to rabies diagnosis in humans or mammals

questions.stem: Which is true about arboviral disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Yellow fever is endemic in India

options.label: B
options.text: Dengue viruses have only one serotype

options.label: D
options.text: Japanese encephalitis is transmitted by Aedes

questions.solutionHtml: n of Incorrect Options: (A) Yellow fever is endemic in India: Incorrect. Yellow fever is not endemic in India. The disease, caused by the Yellow Fever Virus (YFV), a flavivirus, is endemic to sub-Saharan Africa and South America. India has strict vaccination policies for travelers coming from yellow fever-endemic countries to prevent its introduction. Aedes mosquitoes (Aedes aegypti) are the primary vectors of yellow fever. (B) Dengue viruses have only one serotype: Incorrect. Dengue virus (DENV) has four distinct serotypes: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. A person infected with one serotype develops lifelong immunity against that specific serotype but remains susceptible to infection by the other three serotypes. Secondary infections with a different serotype increase the risk of severe dengue (Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever and Dengue Shock Syndrome) due to antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). (D) Japanese encephalitis is transmitted by Aedes: Incorrect. Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV), a flavivirus, is primarily transmitted by Culex mosquitoes (Culex tritaeniorhynchus and Culex vishnui group), not Aedes. These mosquitoes breed in rice fields and stagnant water and primarily transmit JEV in rural areas of Asia. Pigs and water birds act as amplifying hosts, while humans are dead-end hosts.

questions.stem: Mark true in following:

options.label: A
options.text: Hanta virus pulmonary syndrome is caused by inhalation of rodent urine and feces

options.label: B
options.text: Kyasanur forest disease is caused by bite of wild animal

options.label: C
options.text: Lyssa virus is transmitted by ticks

options.label: D
options.text: Lyssa virus is transmitted by ticks

questions.answerText: Hanta virus pulmonary syndrome is caused by inhalation of rodent urine and feces
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Kyasanur forest disease is caused by the bite of a wild animal: Incorrect. Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD) is not transmitted by wild animals but by the bite of infected hard ticks (Haemaphysalis spinigera). KFD is a tick-borne viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the KFD virus (a flavivirus), primarily found in forested areas of India. Monkeys and small mammals serve as reservoirs, but humans contract the disease through tick bites, not wild animal bites. (C) Lyssavirus is transmitted by ticks: Incorrect. Lyssavirus, which includes Rabies virus, is transmitted through the bite or saliva of infected mammals (e.g., dogs, bats, foxes), not ticks. Rabies is a neurotropic viral disease causing fatal encephalitis in humans and animals. The virus spreads through nerve pathways to the central nervous system (CNS), leading to hydrophobia, paralysis, and coma if untreated. Tick bites have no role in rabies transmission. (D) Lyssavirus is transmitted by ticks: Incorrect (repeated). As mentioned above, Lyssavirus (Rabies virus) is not transmitted by ticks but rather through infected animal bites, scratches, or exposure to saliva.

questions.stem: Most specific for Dengue diagnosis
questions.solutionHtml: n of Incorrect Options: (B) Tissue culture: Incorrect. While Dengue virus can be isolated in tissue culture using mosquito cell lines (e.g., C6/36 cells) or mammalian cell cultures (e.g., Vero cells), this method is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and not routinely used for diagnosis. Additionally, virus isolation requires a specialized biosafety level (BSL-2 or BSL-3) laboratory, making it impractical for rapid clinical diagnosis. (C) Complement Fixation Test (CFT): Incorrect. CFT is an older, less specific serological test that detects antibodies against Dengue virus. However, it is not commonly used due to low sensitivity and cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses (e.g., Zika, Japanese Encephalitis). Modern methods like ELISA and RT-PCR have largely replaced CFT for Dengue diagnosis. (D) Electron microscopy: Incorrect. Although electron microscopy (EM) can visualize Dengue virus particles, it is not a practical diagnostic tool because it requires expensive equipment, skilled personnel, and high viral loads in samples. EM is mainly used for research purposes rather than routine clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: All of the following statements are true about congenital rubella except:

options.label: A
options.text: It is diagnosed when the infant has IgM antibodies at birth

options.label: B
options.text: It is diagnosed when IgG antibodies persist for more than 6 months

options.label: C
options.text: MC congenital defects are deafness, cardiac malformation and cataract

options.label: D
options.text: Infection after 16 weeks of gestation result in major congenital defects

questions.answerText: Infection after 16 weeks of gestation result in major congenital defects
questions.solutionHtml: n of Correct Options: (A) It is diagnosed when the infant has IgM antibodies at birth: Correct. Rubella-specific IgM antibodies in a newborn indicate congenital infection, as maternal IgM does not cross the placenta. IgM antibodies appear shortly after infection and persist for a few months in the infant, making them a reliable marker of congenital rubella syndrome. (B) It is diagnosed when IgG antibodies persist for more than 6 months: Correct. While maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and are present in all newborns of rubella-immune mothers, these antibodies typically decline within 6 months. However, in congenital rubella, IgG antibodies persist beyond 6 months due to ongoing viral replication in the infant, confirming the diagnosis of CRS. (C) Most common congenital defects are deafness, cardiac malformations, and cataracts: Correct. The classic triad of congenital rubella syndrome includes sensorineural deafness, congenital heart disease (especially patent ductus arteriosus and pulmonary artery stenosis), and cataracts. Other manifestations include microcephaly, mental retardation, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenic purpura ("blueberry muffin rash"), and intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). Deafness is the most common defect and may occur even if maternal infection occurs later in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 11-month-old child presents with complaints of respiratory distress. On examination there is bilateral crepitation and wheezing. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.solutionHtml: on of Incorrect Options: (A) Pneumonia: Incorrect. While bacterial pneumonia (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) and viral pneumonia (e.g., influenza, adenovirus) can present with respiratory distress and crepitations, wheezing is not a prominent feature in bacterial pneumonia. Instead, pneumonia typically presents with fever, tachypnea, and focal signs like unilateral crackles or bronchial breathing. (B) Adenovirus: Incorrect. Adenovirus can cause pneumonia and bronchiolitis, but it is less common than RSV in infants. Adenoviral infections are often more severe, with a longer duration of symptoms, high fever, and multisystem involvement (e.g., conjunctivitis, gastroenteritis). Unlike RSV, adenovirus is more likely to cause necrotizing pneumonia. (D) Rhinovirus: Incorrect. Rhinovirus is the most common cause of the common cold and can also trigger wheezing episodes, especially in children with a history of asthma or atopy. However, rhinovirus-associated bronchiolitis is less severe compared to RSV, and it is not the leading cause of bronchiolitis in infants.

questions.stem: All are true about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, EXCEPT:

options.label: D
options.text: Recently disease has been reported in Gujarat

questions.solutionHtml: ion of CCHF Facts A. Zoonosis (TRUE): CCHF is a zoonotic disease, meaning it is transmitted to humans from animals, primarily through the bite of an infected tick or by contact with the blood or tissues of infected livestock. B. Develop petechial rashes (TRUE/MOSTLY TRUE in severe cases): As a severe hemorrhagic fever, patients can develop petechiae (small pinprick bleeding spots), along with larger bleeding manifestations like ecchymoses (bruises) and mucosal hemorrhages. While not the defining rash, the presence of petechiae is consistent with the disease's severe bleeding diathesis. C. Transmitted by mites (FALSE): CCHF is primarily transmitted by ticks, particularly those of the Hyalomma genus, which are arachnids but are distinct from mites. D. Recently disease has been reported in Gujarat (TRUE/CONTEXTUALLY PLAUSIBLE): CCHF has been documented in India, with the first major cluster reported in Gujarat in 2011. While "recently" is relative, the disease's presence in that region is a known and medically relevant fact.

questions.stem: In India, human infections have been reported dengue virus type:
questions.solutionHtml: f Incorrect Options: (A) Types I and 1 – Incorrect There is no such classification as “Type I and 1”. The four correct serotypes are DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. This option appears to be a typographical error and is incorrect. (B) Types 1 and 3 – Incorrect Although DENV-1 and DENV-3 are commonly reported in India, DENV-2 and DENV-4 are also present. DENV-2 is often associated with severe outbreaks and has been a major cause of dengue hemorrhagic fever in India. Therefore, this option is incomplete. (C) Types 2 and 4 – Incorrect While DENV-2 and DENV-4 have been detected in India, this option ignores DENV-1 and DENV-3, both of which are also present. DENV-1 is associated with classical dengue fever, whereas DENV-3 has been linked to severe epidemics. Since all four serotypes circulate in India, this answer is incorrect. (D) Type 1 only – Incorrect DENV-1 is one of the serotypes detected in India, but it is not the only one. The circulation of all four serotypes has been documented, and outbreaks have involved multiple serotypes. DENV-2 and DENV-3, in particular, have been responsible for severe outbreaks.

questions.stem: Pre-exposure cell culture vaccine used in Rabies
questions.solutionHtml: f Incorrect Options: (B) 4 doses – Incorrect A 4-dose schedule is not used for pre-exposure prophylaxis. However, in post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), the Essen regimen involves 4 doses of the vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, and 14 (when rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) is given). The 4-dose schedule is not applicable for pre-exposure vaccination. (C) 5 doses – Incorrect The 5-dose regimen (Essen regimen: days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28) is used for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) in individuals who have never been vaccinated against rabies before. This is not the standard regimen for pre-exposure prophylaxis, making this answer incorrect. (D) 6 doses – Incorrect A 6-dose schedule is not recommended for rabies vaccination. Older regimens such as the Milwaukee protocol involved prolonged treatment, but they are not used for routine pre-exposure prophylaxis. Therefore, this option is incorrect.

questions.stem: Diarrrhea in Rotavirus infection is due to:
questions.solutionHtml: f Incorrect Options: (A) Increased intestinal hypermotility – Incorrect Rotavirus infection does not primarily cause diarrhea through increased gut motility. While some viral infections may influence motility, the main mechanism in rotavirus is villous atrophy and malabsorption, not hypermotility. (C) Increased secretion by villi – Incorrect Although some degree of secretory diarrhea occurs due to viral enterotoxin (NSP4 protein), the dominant mechanism is malabsorption due to villous destruction. Unlike bacterial infections like cholera, which cause diarrhea mainly through active secretion, rotavirus diarrhea is more osmotic in nature. (D) None of the above – Incorrect Since decreased absorption by villi (option B) is the correct explanation, this option is incorrect.

questions.stem: Recommended vaccines for rabies:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) DPT – Incorrect DPT (Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus) vaccine is used to protect against bacterial infections caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Bordetella pertussis, and Clostridium tetani. It has no role in rabies prevention, making this option incorrect. (B) MMR – Incorrect MMR (Measles, Mumps, and Rubella) vaccine is used to prevent viral infections caused by measles virus, mumps virus, and rubella virus. It does not provide immunity against rabies, so this option is incorrect. (C) BCG – Incorrect BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) vaccine is used for protection against tuberculosis (TB), particularly in children. It is a live attenuated vaccine derived from Mycobacterium bovis and has no role in preventing rabies, making this option incorrect.

questions.stem: Break bone fever is caused by which virus:
questions.solutionHtml: f Incorrect Options: (A) Variola – Incorrect Variola virus causes smallpox, which is characterized by fever, malaise, and a progressive vesicular rash. It does not cause breakbone fever or severe musculoskeletal pain, making this option incorrect. (B) Coxsackie – Incorrect Coxsackie virus, belonging to the Picornavirus family, causes diseases such as Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease (HFMD), Herpangina, and viral myocarditis. While it can lead to fever and muscle pain, it does not cause the severe bone and joint pain characteristic of dengue fever. (D) Adenovirus – Incorrect Adenovirus primarily causes respiratory infections, conjunctivitis, and gastroenteritis, but it is not associated with breakbone fever or severe musculoskeletal pain.

questions.stem: Commonest cause of Bronchiolitis is:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Adenovirus – Incorrect Adenovirus can cause respiratory infections, pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, and pneumonia, but it is a less common cause of bronchiolitis compared to RSV. While adenovirus infections can contribute to bronchiolitis-like symptoms, they are not the leading cause. (C) Influenza – Incorrect Influenza virus primarily causes influenza (flu), a systemic illness with fever, cough, myalgia, and fatigue. Although influenza virus can cause lower respiratory tract infections, it is not the most common cause of bronchiolitis in infants. (D) Herpesvirus – Incorrect Herpesviruses, including Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV), typically cause vesicular skin and mucosal infections rather than bronchiolitis. HSV can cause severe pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals, but it is not a common cause of bronchiolitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding influenza:

options.label: A
options.text: It is caused by an enveloped DNA virus

options.label: B
options.text: Laboratory studies may show neutropenia early in the course of disease

options.label: C
options.text: Primary infectious pneumonia is less common than secondary bacteria pneumonia

options.label: D
options.text: Antiviral agents are given early prevents complications

questions.answerText: Primary infectious pneumonia is less common than secondary bacteria pneumonia
questions.solutionHtml: n of Incorrect Options: (A) It is caused by an enveloped DNA virus – Incorrect Influenza virus belongs to the Orthomyxoviridae family and is an enveloped, single-stranded, segmented RNA virus, not a DNA virus. The genome segmentation allows for genetic reassortment, which leads to antigenic shifts and drifts, contributing to seasonal flu outbreaks and pandemics. (B) Laboratory studies may show neutropenia early in the course of disease – Incorrect Influenza infection primarily induces a viral response, leading to an increase in lymphocytes rather than neutropenia. While some patients may develop mild leukopenia or a transient drop in neutrophils, neutropenia is not a typical hallmark of influenza infection. (D) Antiviral agents given early prevent complications – Incorrect While antiviral drugs such as Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) and Zanamivir can reduce disease severity and duration if given early (within 48 hours of symptom onset), they do not completely prevent complications, especially in high-risk individuals. Patients with comorbidities, elderly individuals, or those with weakened immunity may still develop pneumonia, ARDS, or other complications, despite early antiviral treatment.

questions.stem: Negri bodies are seen in infections due to:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Poliovirus – Incorrect Poliovirus, a member of the Picornaviridae family, primarily infects motor neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord, leading to poliomyelitis and flaccid paralysis. However, it does not produce Negri bodies. Instead, perivascular inflammation and neuronal degeneration are seen in affected tissues. (C) Herpesvirus – Incorrect Herpesviruses, including Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1 and HSV-2), cause intranuclear Cowdry type A inclusion bodies rather than Negri bodies. HSV infections can lead to herpes encephalitis, but their cytopathic effects differ from those of rabies. (D) Adenovirus – Incorrect Adenoviruses are double-stranded DNA viruses that primarily cause respiratory, ocular, and gastrointestinal infections. They produce intranuclear inclusions, not the intracytoplasmic Negri bodies seen in rabies infections.

questions.stem: A vaccine for rabies was first developed by:
questions.solutionHtml: n of Incorrect Options: (B) Robert Koch – Incorrect Robert Koch was a German physician and microbiologist known for discovering the causative agents of tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), cholera (Vibrio cholerae), and anthrax (Bacillus anthracis). While Koch made significant contributions to bacteriology and disease control, he did not develop a vaccine for rabies. (C) Edward Jenner – Incorrect Edward Jenner, an English physician, is credited with developing the first successful vaccine in history—the smallpox vaccine—in 1796. He used material from cowpox lesions to immunize against smallpox, but his work was unrelated to rabies. (D) Karl Landsteiner – Incorrect Karl Landsteiner was an Austrian immunologist and pathologist best known for discovering the ABO blood group system, which revolutionized blood transfusions. He also contributed to the discovery of poliovirus, but he did not work on rabies vaccine development.

questions.stem: Which of the following viruses is composed of two distinct capsids enclosing the double stranded RNA?
questions.solutionHtml: n of Incorrect Options: (A) Adenovirus – Incorrect Adenoviruses are non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses with a single capsid made up of icosahedral symmetry. Unlike reoviruses, they do not have a double-layered capsid structure or a dsRNA genome. They commonly cause respiratory, gastrointestinal, and conjunctival infections in humans. (C) Herpes virus – Incorrect Herpesviruses are enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses belonging to the Herpesviridae family. They have a single capsid surrounded by a lipid envelope, which contains glycoproteins essential for viral entry into host cells. Examples include Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1, HSV-2), Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV), and Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV). (D) Myxovirus – Incorrect Myxoviruses refer to Orthomyxoviruses (e.g., Influenza viruses) and Paramyxoviruses (e.g., Measles, Mumps, Respiratory Syncytial Virus). These viruses are enveloped, single-stranded RNA viruses and do not have double-stranded RNA or a two-layered capsid.

questions.stem: Rotaviruses are responsible for:

options.label: D
options.text: Respiratory tract infection in immunocompromised individuals

questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Acute nonbacterial gastroenteritis in adults – Incorrect While rotaviruses can cause gastroenteritis, they primarily affect infants and young children. Infections in adults are less common and usually mild, as most adults have developed immunity due to prior exposure. Norovirus, rather than rotavirus, is the more frequent cause of acute nonbacterial gastroenteritis in adults. (C) Teratogenic effects – Incorrect Rotavirus infection does not cause teratogenic effects. Teratogenic viruses are those that cause birth defects when a fetus is exposed during pregnancy. Examples include rubella virus, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Zika virus, but rotavirus is not among them. (D) Respiratory tract infection in immunocompromised individuals – Incorrect Rotavirus primarily targets the gastrointestinal tract, not the respiratory system. While some studies have suggested that rotavirus RNA may be detected in the respiratory tract, it is not a recognized cause of respiratory infections, even in immunocompromised individuals. Instead, viruses such as RSV, influenza, and adenoviruses are more commonly associated with respiratory tract infections in immunocompromised hosts.

questions.stem: Rabies virus is inactivated by:
questions.solutionHtml: n of Incorrect Options: There are no incorrect options in this case, as all the listed agents are valid methods for inactivating the rabies virus.

questions.stem: Antirabies vaccine is prepared by
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Street virus: The term "street virus" refers to naturally occurring wild-type rabies viruses found in infected animals. These viruses are highly virulent and cannot be used for vaccine production because they would cause disease rather than prevent it. (C) Line virus: There is no recognized classification of rabies virus called "line virus." This option is incorrect as it does not refer to any known strain used in vaccine development. (D) Wild virus: Wild viruses are naturally circulating strains of rabies found in infected animals such as dogs, bats, foxes, and raccoons. These viruses are dangerous and not attenuated, making them unsuitable for vaccine production. Instead, fixed strains derived from wild viruses are used after attenuation or inactivation.

questions.stem: Swine flu is caused by:
questions.solutionHtml: f Incorrect Options: (B) H5N1: H5N1 is the avian influenza virus, also known as bird flu. It primarily affects birds and has a high fatality rate in humans when transmitted through direct contact with infected birds, but it does not cause swine flu. (C) H3N1: H3N1 is an influenza subtype that has been detected in animals, but it is not a common cause of human flu outbreaks, including swine flu. (D) H2N3: H2N3 is another influenza A subtype that has been detected in swine but is not known to cause significant human infections or swine flu outbreaks.

questions.stem: Non-enveloped ssRNA virus is:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Poxvirus: Poxviruses (e.g., Variola virus, which causes smallpox) are enveloped DNA viruses, not ssRNA viruses. They are among the largest DNA viruses and replicate in the cytoplasm, unlike most DNA viruses that replicate in the nucleus. (C) Retrovirus: Retroviruses (e.g., HIV, HTLV) are enveloped RNA viruses that contain single-stranded RNA but have a reverse transcriptase enzyme, allowing them to transcribe their RNA into DNA for integration into the host genome. (D) Bunyavirus: Bunyaviruses (e.g., Hantavirus, Rift Valley Fever virus) are enveloped, negative-sense ssRNA viruses that typically have a segmented genome. They are transmitted by arthropods (arboviruses) or rodents.

questions.stem: Most virulent dengue fever strain is:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Dengue virus serotype 1 (DENV-1): While DENV-1 is widespread and can cause severe disease, it is generally less virulent than DENV-2. However, it has been associated with major outbreaks and high transmission rates in certain regions. (C) Dengue virus serotype 3 (DENV-3): DENV-3 can cause severe disease, particularly in secondary infections, but it is usually not as virulent as DENV-2. Some studies have reported DENV-3 to be responsible for large outbreaks, but it is not the most commonly linked serotype to fatal cases. (D) Dengue virus serotype 4 (DENV-4): DENV-4 is generally the least virulent serotype, often associated with mild dengue fever rather than severe complications. It has lower epidemic potential compared to DENV-1, DENV-2, and DENV-3.

questions.stem: Antigenic shift:
questions.solutionHtml: on of Incorrect Options: (A) Occurs every 2-3 years: This statement describes antigenic drift, not antigenic shift. Antigenic shift is unpredictable and occurs less frequently, usually every few decades, leading to pandemics. In contrast, antigenic drift occurs continuously over time and leads to seasonal flu outbreaks. (B) Gradual change over time: This describes antigenic drift, which is the slow accumulation of point mutations in viral genes encoding HA and NA proteins. Antigenic shift, on the other hand, is a sudden and drastic change due to genetic reassortment. (D) Occurs in all influenza viruses: Antigenic shift occurs only in influenza A viruses because they can infect multiple species (humans, birds, pigs, etc.), allowing reassortment between different strains. Influenza B and C viruses do not undergo antigenic shift because they primarily infect humans and do not have multiple host reservoirs for reassortment.

questions.stem: Herpangina is caused by:
questions.solutionHtml: n of Incorrect Options: (B) Rhinoviruses: Rhinoviruses are a major cause of common cold and do not typically cause vesicular or ulcerative lesions in the oropharynx. They primarily infect the nasal mucosa, leading to rhinorrhea, sneezing, and mild sore throat but not herpangina. (C) Myxovirus: The Myxovirus group includes influenza viruses and paramyxoviruses (such as measles, mumps, and parainfluenza viruses), none of which cause herpangina. Influenza viruses mainly affect the respiratory tract, while measles can cause Koplik’s spots, which are different from the vesicular lesions of herpangina. (D) Rabies virus: Rabies virus, a member of the Rhabdoviridae family, causes rabies, a fatal neurological disease, and does not present with oral vesicular lesions. Rabies symptoms include hydrophobia, agitation, and progressive paralysis, which are unrelated to herpangina.

questions.stem: Hemorrhagic fever is caused by:
questions.solutionHtml: on of Incorrect Options: (A) West Nile fever: West Nile virus (WNV) belongs to the Flavivirus genus and is primarily transmitted through mosquito bites (Culex species). While it can cause encephalitis and meningitis, it is not a significant cause of hemorrhagic fever. The majority of WNV infections are asymptomatic or mild, presenting with flu-like symptoms, rash, and neurological complications in severe cases. (B) Sandfly fever: Sandfly fever, also known as Phlebotomus fever, is caused by a Bunyavirus (Toscana virus, Naples virus, and Sicilian virus) and is transmitted by sandflies (Phlebotomus species). It typically causes a self-limiting febrile illness with symptoms like fever, headache, and myalgia, but it does not cause severe hemorrhagic fever.

questions.stem: False about Polio:
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Descending Paralysis. Why A is False Ascending Paralysis: Polio typically causes an ascending paralysis, meaning the muscle weakness and paralysis start in the legs and move upwards towards the trunk and arms. This is the opposite of a descending pattern. Descending Paralysis: A descending pattern of paralysis is characteristic of other neurological conditions, most notably botulism and diphtheria.

questions.stem: Classic tried of congenital rubella includes all except
questions.solutionHtml: of Correct Options: (A) Cataract – Correct Congenital cataracts are one of the most common manifestations of CRS. They result from viral-induced damage to the developing lens during early gestation, leading to lens opacification and visual impairment. (B) Deafness – Correct Sensorineural deafness is the most common and often the most debilitating consequence of CRS. The rubella virus affects the cochlea, leading to permanent hearing loss, which is why rubella vaccination is crucial in pregnant women. (D) CHD (Congenital Heart Disease) – Correct Congenital heart defects, particularly patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and pulmonary artery stenosis, are hallmark findings of CRS. The rubella virus disrupts normal cardiovascular development in utero, leading to these defects. Explanation of Incorrect Option: (C) Retinitis – Incorrect While CRS can cause salt-and-pepper retinopathy, this is not the same as retinitis. Retinitis refers to active retinal inflammation, which is not a typical feature of CRS. Instead, the retinal changes in CRS are atrophic and pigmentary rather than inflammatory.

questions.stem: Most common oncogenic RNA virus
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Picornavirus – Incorrect Picornaviruses are non-enveloped, single-stranded positive-sense RNA viruses that include poliovirus, rhinovirus, and enteroviruses. These viruses do not have any known oncogenic potential. They mainly cause acute infections, such as poliomyelitis and hand-foot-mouth disease, rather than chronic oncogenic transformation. (C) Orthomyxovirus – Incorrect Orthomyxoviruses include the influenza viruses, which cause seasonal flu outbreaks. While influenza infections can lead to secondary bacterial infections and severe complications, they are not oncogenic. They lack mechanisms such as integration into the host genome that are necessary for oncogenesis. (D) Paramyxovirus – Incorrect The paramyxovirus family includes viruses such as measles, mumps, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and parainfluenza virus. These viruses primarily cause respiratory and systemic infections but have no known role in cancer development. Measles virus, for example, is associated with subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) but not malignancy.

questions.stem: Which is enveloped virus?
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (B) Norwalk Virus – Incorrect Norwalk virus (now known as Norovirus) is a member of the Calicivirus family and is non-enveloped. It is a small, round, single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus that primarily causes acute gastroenteritis (viral diarrhea). Unlike enveloped viruses, Norovirus is highly resistant to disinfectants and harsh environmental conditions, making it difficult to eliminate from surfaces and contaminated food sources. (C) Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) – Incorrect Hepatitis A virus belongs to the Picornaviridae family (Hepatovirus genus) and is also a non-enveloped virus. It has a single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome and is transmitted via the fecal-oral route, commonly through contaminated food and water. Due to its lack of an envelope, HAV is resistant to bile acids and detergents, allowing it to survive in the gastrointestinal tract. (D) Adenovirus – Incorrect Adenoviruses belong to the Adenoviridae family and are double-stranded DNA viruses that lack an envelope. They are non-enveloped, icosahedral viruses known for causing respiratory infections, conjunctivitis, and gastroenteritis. Since adenoviruses do not have a lipid envelope, they are highly resistant to disinfectants and environmental stress, making them more persistent on surfaces.

questions.stem: The vector of Japanese B encephalitis virus is :
questions.solutionHtml: on of the Correct Answer: The Culex mosquito, particularly Culex tritaeniorhynchus, is the primary vector of Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV), which is a flavivirus responsible for Japanese Encephalitis (JE). Transmission Cycle: Culex mosquitoes become infected when they feed on birds and pigs, which serve as the natural reservoirs of JEV. The virus then multiplies within the mosquito and is transmitted to humans through mosquito bites. Humans are dead-end hosts because they do not develop high enough viremia to continue the transmission cycle. Epidemiology: JEV is endemic in parts of Asia and the Western Pacific. It is more common in rural and agricultural areas, particularly where rice fields and pig farming provide ideal breeding grounds for Culex mosquitoes. Clinical Features of Japanese Encephalitis: Most infections are asymptomatic. Severe cases present with high fever, headache, vomiting, seizures, and altered mental status, potentially leading to coma and death. Neurological sequelae are common in survivors. Prevention: Mosquito control measures (eliminating breeding sites, insecticides, nets). Vaccination is available and recommended for travelers to endemic areas.

questions.stem: Diagnostic of Rabies
questions.solutionHtml: ion of the Correct Answer: Negri bodies are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions found in neurons of the central nervous system, particularly in the hippocampus (pyramidal cells) and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum. They are pathognomonic for Rabies virus infection, caused by Lyssavirus (Rhabdoviridae family). Rabies Diagnosis: Negri bodies can be detected in brain tissue post-mortem using histopathology and immunofluorescence staining. Direct Fluorescent Antibody Test (DFA) is the gold standard for confirming Rabies virus in CNS tissues. RT-PCR and Serology (detecting anti-rabies antibodies in CSF) are used for antemortem diagnosis. Skin biopsy (nuchal region) and saliva testing can also help diagnose Rabies. Rabies Clinical Features: Furious Rabies: Hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation, hypersalivation, spasms. Paralytic Rabies: Flaccid paralysis, confusion, coma, death. Once symptoms appear, rabies is nearly 100% fatal. Treatment & Prevention: No effective treatment once symptoms appear. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP): Rabies vaccine + Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) if exposure is severe. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP): Rabies vaccine for high-risk groups (veterinarians, animal handlers). Explanation of Incorrect Options: (A) Guarneri Bodies – Incorrect Guarneri bodies are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions seen in smallpox (Variola virus) infections. These inclusions are found in epithelial cells of skin lesions in smallpox. (C) Cowdry A Bodies – Incorrect Cowdry A bodies are intranuclear eosinophilic inclusions seen in Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) infections. Found in infected cells of the brain and skin lesions, they are NOT associated with Rabies. (D) Cowdry B Bodies – Incorrect Cowdry B bodies are basophilic intranuclear inclusions seen in Poliovirus and Adenovirus infections. These inclusions are found in infected nerve cells, but they do not play a role in Rabies diagnosis.

questions.stem: Arbovirus – True is

options.label: A
options.text: Yellow fever is endemic in India

options.label: C
options.text: KFD was first identified in West Bengal

questions.solutionHtml: on of the Correct Answer: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is an arbovirus (arthropod-borne virus) belonging to the Togaviridae family, Alphavirus genus. It is primarily transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, specifically: Aedes aegypti (urban areas) Aedes albopictus (rural and semi-urban areas) The virus causes Chikungunya fever, which is characterized by: High fever, polyarthritis/polyarthralgia (often severe and persistent), maculopapular rash, and myalgia. Joint pain can last for weeks to months, mimicking rheumatoid arthritis. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive with hydration, analgesics, and rest. Prevention relies on mosquito control measures and personal protective measures. Explanation of Incorrect Options: (A) Yellow fever is endemic in India – Incorrect Yellow fever virus (YFV) belongs to the Flavivirus genus and is transmitted by Aedes and Haemagogus mosquitoes. It is NOT endemic in India because India has strict quarantine and vaccination policies preventing its spread. Yellow fever is endemic in Africa and South America. Travelers to endemic areas must get the yellow fever vaccine (live-attenuated 17D strain). (B) Dengue has only one serotype – Incorrect Dengue virus (DENV) belongs to the Flavivirus genus and has four distinct serotypes (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, DENV-4). Infection with one serotype provides lifelong immunity to that serotype but not to the others. Secondary infection with a different serotype increases the risk of severe dengue (Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever/Dengue Shock Syndrome) due to antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). (C) KFD was first identified in West Bengal – Incorrect Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD) is a tick-borne viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the KFD virus (KFDV), a Flavivirus. It was first identified in 1957 in Karnataka (Kyasanur Forest, Western Ghats, India), not in West Bengal. KFD is transmitted by Haemaphysalis ticks and is associated with monkeys as reservoir hosts. Prevention includes the KFD vaccine and tick bite precautions.

questions.stem: Which of the viral disease is tick borne
questions.solutionHtml: ion of the Correct Answer: Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD) is a tick-borne viral disease caused by the Kyasanur Forest Disease Virus (KFDV), a member of the Flavivirus genus within the Flaviviridae family. It was first identified in 1957 in the Kyasanur Forest of Karnataka, India. Vector: The virus is transmitted by the bite of Haemaphysalis spinigera ticks. Reservoir Hosts: Monkeys (hence the name "monkey fever"), rodents, and shrews act as natural reservoirs. Clinical Features: Sudden high fever, chills, headache, severe myalgia, and vomiting Hemorrhagic manifestations (epistaxis, gum bleeding, GI bleeding) Neurological symptoms in severe cases Prevention: KFD vaccine is available for high-risk populations in endemic areas. Tick bite prevention measures (protective clothing, insect repellents). Explanation of Incorrect Options: (B) Chikungunya – Incorrect Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) belongs to the Togaviridae family (Alphavirus genus). It is NOT tick-borne; it is transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. Causes high fever, severe polyarthritis/polyarthralgia, maculopapular rash, but no hemorrhagic features. (C) Yellow fever – Incorrect Yellow fever virus (YFV) is a Flavivirus, but it is transmitted by mosquitoes (Aedes and Haemagogus spp.), not ticks. It is endemic in Africa and South America, but not in India. Characterized by jaundice, fever, hemorrhagic symptoms, and multi-organ failure. Prevention: Live-attenuated yellow fever vaccine (17D strain). (D) Dengue – Incorrect Dengue virus (DENV) is another Flavivirus, transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, not ticks. Dengue presents with high fever, retro-orbital pain, severe body aches ("breakbone fever"), rash, and hemorrhagic manifestations in severe cases. No tick involvement in transmission.

questions.stem: Genetic reassortment is found in
questions.solutionHtml: ion of the Correct Answer: Rotavirus belongs to the Reoviridae family and is a segmented, double-stranded RNA virus. Genetic reassortment occurs in viruses that have segmented genomes, where segments from different strains can mix when co-infection happens in the same host cell. This process leads to the emergence of new viral strains, which can contribute to antigenic shift and increased virulence. Rotavirus has an 11-segmented genome, making it capable of genetic reassortment when two different strains infect the same cell. This reassortment plays a significant role in the evolution of rotaviruses, leading to new antigenic variants that may escape immune detection. Rotavirus is a major cause of severe diarrhea in infants and young children worldwide, leading to dehydration and hospitalization. The development of live-attenuated vaccines (Rotarix, RotaTeq) has been instrumental in reducing the disease burden. Explanation of Incorrect Options: (A) Hepadnavirus – Incorrect Hepadnaviruses, such as Hepatitis B Virus (HBV), have a partially double-stranded DNA genome and do not undergo genetic reassortment. HBV undergoes reverse transcription but does not have a segmented genome required for reassortment. (B) Parvovirus – Incorrect Parvoviruses, including Parvovirus B19, have a single-stranded DNA genome and do not have segments, meaning reassortment is not possible. Instead of reassortment, parvoviruses replicate using host cell DNA polymerase. (D) Astrovirus – Incorrect Astroviruses are non-segmented, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses, meaning they cannot undergo reassortment. They primarily cause mild gastroenteritis in children and immunocompromised individuals.-

questions.stem: Chlorination does not affect
questions.solutionHtml: ion of the Correct Answer: Chlorination is a widely used method for disinfecting water, effectively killing or inactivating most bacteria and many viruses. However, poliovirus is highly resistant to chlorination, requiring higher doses and longer exposure times to be completely inactivated. Enteroviruses, including poliovirus, have a strong protein coat (capsid) that makes them more resistant to chlorination compared to other microorganisms. Standard chlorination levels used in drinking water treatment may not always be sufficient to eliminate poliovirus. Additional water purification steps, such as filtration or ultraviolet (UV) treatment, may be needed to ensure complete removal. Thus, poliovirus is not effectively eliminated by normal chlorination, making option (D) the correct answer. Explanation of Incorrect Options: (A) Salmonella – Incorrect Salmonella is a gram-negative bacterium that is highly sensitive to chlorination. Even at standard chlorine levels used in water treatment, Salmonella is effectively killed, making chlorination an important control measure for preventing typhoid fever and salmonellosis. (B) Shigella – Incorrect Shigella, another gram-negative bacterial pathogen, is also highly susceptible to chlorination. Proper chlorination in water systems effectively destroys Shigella, reducing the risk of shigellosis (bacillary dysentery) outbreaks. (C) HIV – Incorrect HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) is an enveloped RNA virus, making it extremely sensitive to disinfectants, including chlorine. Even low levels of chlorine are enough to completely inactivate HIV, preventing transmission through water sources.

questions.stem: A 9- Month-old infant presents to the ‘diarrhea clinic’ unit with some dehydration. The most likely organism causing diarrhea is:
questions.solutionHtml: ion of the Correct Answer: Rotavirus is the most common cause of diarrhea in infants and young children worldwide. Rotavirus primarily affects children aged 6 months to 2 years and is a major cause of severe dehydrating diarrhea in infants. It is a double-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Reoviridae family and spreads through the fecal-oral route. Clinical Features: Watery diarrhea (without blood or mucus). Vomiting and fever (common initial symptoms). Severe dehydration (leading to hospitalization in many cases). Pathogenesis: The virus infects and destroys the intestinal villi, leading to malabsorption and osmotic diarrhea. It also produces the NSP4 enterotoxin, which increases chloride secretion and further contributes to diarrhea. Diagnosis: Rapid antigen detection test (ELISA) in stool RT-PCR for viral RNA detection Prevention: Rotavirus vaccine (part of routine immunization in many countries) Improved sanitation and handwashing Thus, Rotavirus is the most likely cause of diarrhea in this 9-month-old infant presenting with dehydration. Explanation of Incorrect Options: (A) Entamoeba histolytica – Incorrect Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery, which is more common in older children and adults rather than infants. It typically causes bloody diarrhea with mucus (dysentery) rather than watery diarrhea. It is a protozoan parasite transmitted via contaminated water or food. Complications: Amoebic liver abscess Ulceration of the intestinal mucosa Since this infant has watery diarrhea without blood, E. histolytica is unlikely. (C) Giardia lamblia – Incorrect Giardia lamblia is a protozoan parasite that causes chronic diarrhea rather than acute, severe dehydration. Symptoms: Foul-smelling, greasy stools (steatorrhea) Malabsorption and weight loss No fever or severe dehydration More common in older children and adults, especially those exposed to contaminated water. Since the infant has acute diarrhea with dehydration, Giardia is not the most likely cause. (D) Shigella – Incorrect Shigella causes bacterial dysentery (Shigellosis), which is characterized by: Bloody, mucus-containing diarrhea (not purely watery diarrhea). Severe abdominal cramps and high fever. It is more common in toddlers and preschool children rather than infants. Shigella invades the colonic mucosa, leading to inflammation and tissue destruction. Complications: Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS) (especially with Shigella dysenteriae). Since this infant has watery diarrhea with dehydration (not bloody diarrhea), Shigella is unlikely.

questions.stem: Echoviruses are cytopathogenic human viruses that mainly infect which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml: ion of the Correct Answer: Echoviruses are members of the Enterovirus genus in the Picornaviridae family. These viruses are cytopathogenic (meaning they cause cell damage) and primarily affect the central nervous system (CNS). They are one of the leading causes of aseptic meningitis, especially in children. Other neurological manifestations include encephalitis and paralysis, though these are less common. Echoviruses spread through the fecal-oral route and initially replicate in the gastrointestinal tract before spreading systemically via the bloodstream (viremia), allowing CNS invasion. Thus, echoviruses primarily infect the CNS, making option (C) the correct answer. Explanation of Incorrect Options: (A) Bladder and urinary tract – Incorrect Echoviruses do not have a primary affinity for the bladder or urinary tract. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are typically caused by bacteria such as E. coli and not by enteroviruses. (B) Blood and lymphatic system – Incorrect While echoviruses do enter the bloodstream (viremia) to reach target organs, they do not primarily infect or replicate in the blood or lymphatic system. Their main targets are the CNS, heart (myocarditis), skin (rash), and GI tract. (D) Respiratory system – Incorrect Echoviruses do not primarily target the respiratory system. Some enteroviruses, like Enterovirus D68, can cause respiratory infections, but echoviruses typically lead to neurological, gastrointestinal, or cardiac manifestations, rather than respiratory illness.

questions.stem: A 10 year old boy is taken to his pediatrician after experiencing fever, malaise, and anorexia,followed by tender swelling of his parotid glands. Mumps was diagnosed on clinical presentation.Which of the following characterizes infection by this virus?

options.label: A
options.text: Is apt recur periodically in many affected persons

options.label: B
options.text: Is maintained by a large canine reservoir

questions.solutionHtml: ion of the Correct Answer: Mumps is caused by the Mumps virus, a Paramyxovirus that spreads via respiratory droplets and primarily affects the parotid glands. Infection is characterized by fever, malaise, and painful parotitis. Mumps is preventable through immunization with the MMR (Measles, Mumps, and Rubella) vaccine, which contains a live attenuated form of the virus. The MMR vaccine is administered in two doses (first at 12-15 months, second at 4-6 years), providing long-lasting immunity. Due to widespread vaccination, mumps has become rare in many parts of the world. Thus, vaccination is the key preventive measure, making option (C) the correct answer. Explanation of Incorrect Options: (A) Is apt to recur periodically in many affected persons – Incorrect Mumps does not typically recur because infection (or vaccination) induces long-lasting immunity. Unlike herpesviruses, which establish latency and reactivate periodically, mumps does not persist in the body after infection. (B) Is maintained by a large canine reservoir – Incorrect Mumps is a human-specific virus and has no animal reservoir, including dogs or other canines. The virus spreads exclusively from human to human via respiratory droplets. (D) Usually produces severe systemic manifestations – Incorrect Mumps is usually self-limiting and resolves without complications. However, in some cases, it can cause complications like orchitis (testicular inflammation in males), meningitis, pancreatitis, and deafness. Despite potential complications, severe systemic disease is not the norm. (E) Belongs to Orthomyxovirus – Incorrect The Mumps virus belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family. Orthomyxoviruses include Influenza viruses, which have a different genetic structure (segmented RNA genome) and a different mode of replication.

questions.stem: Two siblings, ages 2 and 4, experienced fever, rhinitis, and pharyngitis that resulted inlaryngotrachiobronchitis. Both had harsh cough and hoarseness. Which virus is could beresponsible for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml: ion of the Correct Answer: The children in this case are experiencing laryngotracheobronchitis, commonly known as croup, characterized by fever, rhinitis, pharyngitis, a harsh barking cough, and hoarseness. Croup is most commonly caused by the Parainfluenza virus, specifically types 1 and 2, which belong to the Paramyxoviridae family. The virus spreads via respiratory droplets and affects the upper respiratory tract, leading to inflammation of the larynx, trachea, and bronchi. Characteristic features of croup include: Inspiratory stridor (a harsh, high-pitched sound due to airway obstruction) Barking cough (often compared to a seal’s bark) Hoarseness due to vocal cord inflammation "Steeple sign" on X-ray (narrowing of the subglottic region of the trachea) Parainfluenza virus is the leading cause of viral croup in young children, making it the correct answer. Explanation of Incorrect Options: (A) Adenovirus – Incorrect Adenoviruses cause respiratory infections, pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, and gastroenteritis, but they are not the primary cause of croup. Unlike Parainfluenza virus, Adenovirus does not typically cause the barking cough and stridor seen in croup. (B) Group B Coxsackievirus – Incorrect Group B Coxsackieviruses are known to cause pleurodynia (Bornholm disease), myocarditis, and pericarditis, rather than croup. Coxsackievirus A, not Group B, is associated with herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease. (D & E) Rhinovirus – Incorrect Rhinovirus is the most common cause of the common cold and can cause upper respiratory infections. However, it does not typically cause croup, as it does not induce significant laryngotracheal inflammation.

questions.stem: All are true about Influenza A virus except

options.label: A
options.text: May cause antigenic shift and antigenic drift

questions.solutionHtml: on of the Correct Answer: Influenza A virus is known for its high genetic variability, which makes lifelong protection from a single vaccination impossible. The influenza vaccine needs to be updated annually due to: Antigenic drift – Small genetic mutations in the hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) proteins lead to gradual changes, making previous immunity ineffective over time. Antigenic shift – A sudden and major genetic reassortment in the virus, creating a completely new strain that can lead to pandemics. Because of these changes, influenza vaccines provide only temporary protection (typically for one flu season), and annual vaccination is recommended. Hence, option (C) is incorrect and is the correct answer to this "except" question. Explanation of Incorrect Options: (A) May cause antigenic shift and antigenic drift – Correct ? Influenza A virus undergoes both: Antigenic drift – Minor genetic mutations occur frequently, leading to seasonal flu outbreaks. Antigenic shift – A major genetic reassortment between different influenza strains (often between human and animal strains), which can result in pandemics (e.g., H1N1 in 2009). Since Influenza A is the only type capable of antigenic shift, this statement is correct. (B) May cause pandemics – Correct ? Influenza A is responsible for all major flu pandemics due to its ability to undergo antigenic shift. Examples include: 1918 Spanish flu (H1N1) 1957 Asian flu (H2N2) **1968 Hong Kong flu (H3

questions.stem: All are true about Respiratory Syncytial Viruses except:
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) May cause bronchiolitis – Correct RSV is a leading cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants and young children. It infects the lower respiratory tract, causing inflammation, mucus production, and airway obstruction, leading to difficulty in breathing, wheezing, and cough. (B) Is an RNA virus – Correct RSV is a single-stranded, negative-sense RNA virus belonging to the family Paramyxoviridae. Like other RNA viruses, it relies on RNA-dependent RNA polymerase for replication. (D) Belongs to Paramyxovirus – Correct RSV is classified under the Paramyxoviridae family, Pneumoviridae subfamily, along with other respiratory pathogens like human metapneumovirus. It shares structural and replication characteristics with other paramyxoviruses, such as fusion proteins that facilitate viral entry into host cells.

questions.stem: Acute infantile diarrhea is most commonly due to infection with which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Rotaviruses. Rotavirus is the most common cause of acute infantile diarrhea worldwide, particularly in children under 5 years of age, with the highest incidence in infants between 6 months and 2 years old. It is a double-stranded RNA virus from the Reoviridae family and is highly contagious, spreading primarily through the fecal-oral route. Rotavirus infects and damages the small intestinal villi, leading to malabsorption and secretory diarrhea due to the action of NSP4 enterotoxin, which increases chloride secretion. The illness typically presents with watery diarrhea, vomiting, and fever, and can lead to severe dehydration, which is a major cause of childhood mortality in developing countries. Vaccination (e.g., Rotarix, RotaTeq) has significantly reduced its burden, but outbreaks still occur. Incorrect options: (A) Enteroviruses – Incorrect. Enteroviruses (e.g., Coxsackievirus, Echovirus, Poliovirus) are members of the Picornaviridae family and primarily cause illnesses such as herpangina, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, viral meningitis, and myocarditis. While some enteroviruses can cause gastrointestinal symptoms, they are not the leading cause of acute infantile diarrhea. (C) Noroviruses – Incorrect. Noroviruses are a common cause of viral gastroenteritis, especially in older children and adults. They are responsible for outbreaks in closed communities (e.g., cruise ships, schools, nursing homes). Although norovirus can cause diarrhea in infants, rotavirus remains the predominant cause in this age group. (D) Enteric adenoviruses – Incorrect. Enteric adenoviruses (types 40 and 41) can cause diarrhea in children, but they are a less common cause compared to rotavirus. Adenovirus-related diarrhea is typically less severe and prolonged compared to rotavirus and lacks the characteristic seasonal outbreaks associated with rotavirus infections.

questions.stem: Detection of Dengue within 5 days can be done by
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) NS1 Antigen detection. In dengue infection, NS1 (Non-Structural Protein 1) antigen detection is the preferred test for diagnosing dengue within the first 5 days of illness (acute phase). NS1 is a viral protein secreted into the bloodstream by actively replicating dengue virus, making it an early marker of infection. It is detectable in serum from day 1 to day 5 before the appearance of antibodies. NS1 antigen ELISA or rapid immunochromatographic (ICT) tests are commonly used for early dengue diagnosis. Incorrect options: (B) MAC ELISA – Incorrect. MAC ELISA detects IgM antibodies against dengue, which typically appear after 4–5 days of illness. Since it is an antibody-based test, it is not useful for very early detection in the first few days of infection. (C) ICT test to detect IgM – Incorrect. IgM detection by ICT (Immunochromatographic Test) is similar to MAC ELISA in that it detects IgM antibodies. Since IgM levels rise after 5 days of infection, this test is not useful for early diagnosis. (D) None of the above – Incorrect. NS1 antigen detection is the best option for early dengue diagnosis, so choosing "None of the above" would be incorrect.

questions.answerText: Accumulated small mutations can change viral antigens

Correct answer: E - Accumulated small mutations can change viral antigens
