questions.stem: Which of the following statement is true regarding arboviruses

options.label: A
options.text: Yellow fever is endemic in India

options.label: B
options.text: Dengue virus has only one serotype

options.label: C
options.text: Kyasanur forest disease (KFD) is transmitted by ticks

options.label: D
options.text: Mosquito of culexvishnui complex is the vector of dengue fever

questions.answerText: Kyasanur forest disease (KFD) is transmitted by ticks
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Kyasanur forest disease (KFD) is transmitted by ticks. Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD) is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Kyasanur Forest Disease Virus (KFDV), a Flavivirus. It is endemic to India, particularly in the forested regions of Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu. The primary vector responsible for transmitting KFD is ticks, mainly Haemaphysalis spinigera. The disease is transmitted through the bite of infected ticks and can also spread through contact with infected animals such as monkeys, rodents, and cattle. The symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pain, bleeding tendencies, and neurological complications in severe cases. Incorrect options: (A) Yellow fever is endemic in India – Incorrect. Yellow fever, caused by the Yellow Fever Virus (a Flavivirus) and transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, is not endemic in India. While it is prevalent in Africa and South America, India has never reported a case of yellow fever due to strict vaccination and quarantine regulations for travelers from endemic areas. (B) Dengue virus has only one serotype – Incorrect. Dengue virus (DENV) actually has four serotypes (DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4). Infection with one serotype provides lifelong immunity against that specific serotype but only partial and temporary protection against the others. Subsequent infections with a different serotype can lead to severe complications, including Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever (DHF) and Dengue Shock Syndrome (DSS) due to antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). (D) Mosquito of Culex vishnui complex is the vector of dengue fever – Incorrect. Dengue fever is transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, not Culex mosquitoes. Culex vishnui complex (Culex tritaeniorhynchus, Culex vishnui, and Culex pseudovishnui) is responsible for Japanese Encephalitis (JE) transmission. (E) Japanese encephalitis is transmitted by Aedes – Incorrect. Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV), a Flavivirus, is transmitted primarily by Culex mosquitoes, especially Culex tritaeniorhynchus, not Aedes. JEV is endemic in many parts of Asia, including India, and causes viral encephalitis, leading to neurological complications in severe cases.

questions.stem: Human to human transmission is not seen in
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Japanese B encephalitis because human-to-human transmission is not seen in this disease. Japanese B encephalitis (JBE) is caused by the Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), a flavivirus, which is primarily transmitted by Culex mosquitoes (especially Culex tritaeniorhynchus). Humans are dead-end hosts, meaning that even if an infected mosquito bites a human, the virus does not reach high enough levels in human blood to allow further transmission to another mosquito. Hence, JBE does not spread from one human to another. Incorrect Options: (A) SARS – Incorrect Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS), caused by the SARS-CoV coronavirus, spreads readily from human to human through respiratory droplets, close contact, and contaminated surfaces (fomites). (C) H5N1 – Incorrect H5N1 is a highly pathogenic avian influenza virus that primarily infects birds. However, limited human-to-human transmission has been reported in close-contact settings, such as family clusters. The risk of sustained human-to-human transmission is low, but it is still possible. (D) Poliomyelitis – Incorrect Poliovirus, an enterovirus, spreads easily between humans through the fecal-oral route, often due to contaminated food and water. It can also spread via the oral-oral route through respiratory secretions. (E) HIV – Incorrect Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) is transmitted exclusively from human to human through blood, sexual contact, vertical transmission (mother to child), and contaminated needles. It does not spread through casual contact.

questions.stem: Natural reservoir of Hendra virus is
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Bat because the natural reservoir of the Hendra virus (HeV) is fruit bats (flying foxes) of the Pteropodidae family. Hendra virus is a zoonotic paramyxovirus that was first identified in 1994 in Australia. While bats do not show symptoms of the disease, they shed the virus in their urine, saliva, feces, and birthing fluids, which can contaminate the environment and infect other animals, particularly horses. Horses serve as an intermediate host and can transmit the virus to humans through direct contact with infected bodily fluids. Human infections are rare but can be fatal, causing severe respiratory and neurological diseases. Incorrect Options: (A) Horse – Incorrect Horses are not the natural reservoir of Hendra virus; they act as an intermediate host. The virus spreads from bats to horses and then may be transmitted to humans through close contact. (B) Man – Incorrect Humans are accidental hosts and can contract the infection through contact with infected horses, but they do not act as a reservoir for the virus. (D) Pig – Incorrect Pigs are not associated with Hendra virus transmission. However, a closely related virus, Nipah virus, also found in bats, has been transmitted through pigs in past outbreaks. (E) Duck – Incorrect Ducks and other birds are not involved in Hendra virus transmission or reservoir maintenance. The virus is primarily bat-borne with secondary transmission through horses.

questions.stem: All of the following statements are true regarding polio- virus except:

options.label: A
options.text: It is transmitted by Feco-oral route

options.label: B
options.text: Asymptomatic infections are common in children

options.label: C
options.text: There is a single serotype causing infection

options.label: D
options.text: Live attenuated vaccine produces herd immunity

questions.answerText: There is a single serotype causing infection
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) There is a single serotype causing infection, which is incorrect. Poliovirus has three distinct serotypes: Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3. Each serotype is antigenically different, meaning infection with one serotype does not provide immunity against the others. Among them, Type 1 is the most commonly associated with paralytic polio, while Type 2 has been eradicated globally. The presence of multiple serotypes makes vaccine development and immunization efforts more complex, requiring trivalent or bivalent vaccines for protection against all circulating strains. Incorrect Options (True Statements): (A) Poliovirus is transmitted by the fecal-oral route – True Poliovirus is primarily transmitted through the fecal-oral route, especially in areas with poor sanitation. The virus replicates in the gastrointestinal tract, spreads through contaminated food, water, or hands, and can then reach the central nervous system, leading to poliomyelitis. (B) Asymptomatic infections are common in children – True The majority of poliovirus infections are asymptomatic, particularly in children. Only about 1% of cases progress to paralytic poliomyelitis, while most individuals develop immunity without noticeable symptoms. Some may experience mild flu-like symptoms such as fever, sore throat, or gastrointestinal upset. (D) Live attenuated vaccine produces herd immunity – True The Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV), a live attenuated vaccine, induces both mucosal and systemic immunity. By replicating in the intestines, it helps prevent viral shedding and transmission, thereby providing herd immunity. This is a key advantage over the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), which primarily provides individual protection without stopping transmission as effectively.

questions.stem: All of the following clinical features are associated with enteroviruses except:
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Hemorrhagic fever, which is not a clinical feature commonly associated with enteroviruses. Enteroviruses belong to the Picornaviridae family and primarily cause diseases affecting the gastrointestinal tract, central nervous system, heart, and respiratory system. While enteroviruses can cause a wide range of clinical syndromes, they are not typically associated with hemorrhagic fever. Hemorrhagic fevers are caused by viruses such as Dengue virus, Ebola virus, Marburg virus, and Lassa virus, which primarily lead to vascular leakage, bleeding tendencies, and multi-organ failure, unlike enteroviruses. Incorrect Options (True Statements): (A) Myocarditis – True Enteroviruses, particularly Coxsackie B virus, are well-known causes of viral myocarditis, which leads to inflammation of the heart muscle. It can present with chest pain, arrhythmias, heart failure, or sudden cardiac death, especially in young adults. (B) Pleurodynia – True Also known as Bornholm disease or Devil’s grip, pleurodynia is caused by Coxsackie B virus. It presents with severe, sudden-onset chest or abdominal pain, worsened by breathing or movement, and is due to inflammation of the intercostal muscles and pleura. (C) Herpangina – True Herpangina is a viral illness caused by Coxsackie A virus, characterized by painful vesicular lesions in the oropharynx, fever, and sore throat. It primarily affects children and is highly contagious.

questions.stem: All are false regarding polio virus except:

options.label: C
options.text: Inactivated polio vaccines are given to child less than 3 years of age

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (B) Inactivated vaccine given I/M. Inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) is given via the intramuscular (I/M) or subcutaneous (S/C) route. It contains killed poliovirus strains of all three serotypes and is used in many countries as part of routine immunization programs. IPV induces systemic immunity by stimulating the production of serum antibodies, which prevent the virus from spreading to the central nervous system and causing paralysis. It is an important component of polio eradication efforts, especially in areas where the oral polio vaccine (OPV) carries the risk of vaccine-derived poliovirus. Incorrect Options (False Statements): (A) Most cases are symptomatic – False Contrary to this statement, most polio infections are asymptomatic. Approximately 90-95% of polio cases are subclinical, meaning infected individuals do not show symptoms. Only 1% of cases progress to paralytic polio, while the remaining cases may have mild flu-like symptoms. (C) Inactivated polio vaccines are given to children less than 3 years of age – False IPV is part of childhood immunization schedules, but it is not exclusively given to children under 3 years. It is administered as a series of doses (at 2, 4, and 6–18 months, followed by a booster at 4–6 years) and can also be given to adults in high-risk situations. (D) Only one type exists – False There are three serotypes of poliovirus (Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3). While Type 2 was declared eradicated in 2015, and Type 3 in 2019, Type 1 still circulates in some regions. This diversity is why polio vaccines must contain all three serotypes to ensure full protection.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman with a history of diabetes presents with left ear pain and drainage of pus from the ear canal. She has swelling and tenderness over the left mastoid bone. Which of the following microorganisms is the most likely causative agent?
questions.solutionHtml: ion for the Correct Answer: The most likely causative agent in this case is Pseudomonas aeruginosa, as the patient's presentation suggests malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa (MOE), a severe infection of the external auditory canal that extends to the skull base. Risk factors for MOE include diabetes mellitus and immunocompromised states. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common pathogen responsible for MOE, accounting for more than 90% of cases. The infection typically presents with severe ear pain, purulent otorrhea, and tenderness over the mastoid. If untreated, it can progress to osteomyelitis of the skull base and cranial nerve involvement. Due to its strong virulence factors, antibiotic resistance, and ability to thrive in moist environments, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the leading cause of severe external ear infections in elderly diabetic patients. Explanation for Incorrect Options: (A) Haemophilus influenzae – Incorrect H. influenzae is a common cause of otitis media in children but not malignant otitis externa. It is usually associated with upper respiratory tract infections and is not the primary pathogen in diabetic patients with severe ear infections. (B) Klebsiella pneumoniae – Incorrect Klebsiella pneumoniae is more commonly associated with pneumonia and urinary tract infections. It is not a typical cause of malignant otitis externa. (C) Mucor spp. – Incorrect Mucor species cause mucormycosis, an opportunistic fungal infection in immunocompromised patients. Although diabetic patients are at risk for rhinocerebral mucormycosis, the typical presentation includes facial necrosis, sinus involvement, and black eschar, not ear pain and purulent drainage. Fungal infections like mucormycosis do not typically cause MOE.

questions.stem: A 32-yea r-old woman who ha d not received the usual pediatric vaccinations developed fever, headache, malaise, and ear pain accompanied by swelling of the pa roti d glands . One week later, her fever subsided but she developed pelvic pain and tenderness . With which virus was she infected?
questions.solutionHtml: of Incorrect Options: (A) Cytomegalovirus (CMV): CMV infection can cause fever, malaise, and organ involvement, but it does not typically cause parotitis or oophoritis. In immunocompromised individuals, CMV can lead to retinitis, pneumonia, or hepatitis, none of which are described in this case. (C) Rabies virus: Rabies presents with severe neurological symptoms such as hydrophobia, agitation, hypersalivation, and paralysis, rather than parotid swelling and pelvic pain. Rabies is transmitted through animal bites and has a long incubation period, making it an unlikely cause in this case. (D) Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV): RSV primarily affects the respiratory tract, causing bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants and young children. It does not cause parotid gland swelling or oophoritis, making it an incorrect choice.

questions.stem: All of the following viruses have been implicated as a cause of human cancer EXCEPT:
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (A) Dengue fever virus. Dengue fever virus has not been implicated in the development of human cancer. Dengue primarily causes acute febrile illness with symptoms like fever, rash, muscle pain, and sometimes hemorrhagic complications. It does not have a known link to oncogenesis or the development of cancer in humans. Therefore, it is the exception in this list of viruses that are associated with cancer. Incorrect Options: (B) Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is strongly associated with several types of human cancers, including Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and stomach cancer. EBV is a herpesvirus that can immortalize infected B cells and has been implicated in the development of lymphoproliferative disorders. Therefore, it is correctly included as a virus linked to cancer. (C) Hepatitis B virus (HBV) Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a well-established carcinogen and is strongly linked to the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a primary liver cancer. Chronic infection with HBV can lead to liver cirrhosis and eventually liver cancer. The HBV virus integrates into the host genome, promoting mutations that contribute to carcinogenesis. Hence, HBV is rightly listed as a cancer-causing virus. (D) Hepatitis C virus (HCV) Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is also associated with an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), particularly in individuals with chronic HCV infection. Chronic inflammation caused by HCV infection can lead to liver cirrhosis, which is a precursor to liver cancer. Therefore, HCV is correctly identified as a cancer-causing virus.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding administration of varicella-zoster vaccine to patients above the age of 60 is true?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a killed virus vaccine, so it is safe in immunocompromised patients

options.label: B
options.text: It is not recommended for patients in this age group

options.label: C
options.text: It will decrease the risk of developing postherpetic neuralgia.

options.label: D
options.text: It will not decrease the risk of developing shingles

questions.answerText: It will decrease the risk of developing postherpetic neuralgia.
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) It will decrease the risk of developing postherpetic neuralgia. The varicella-zoster vaccine (also known as the shingles vaccine) is recommended for adults over the age of 60 to reduce the risk of shingles (herpes zoster) and postherpetic neuralgia (PHN), a debilitating nerve pain that can persist for months or years after a shingles outbreak. Studies have shown that vaccination significantly lowers the incidence of PHN by about 67%, making it an essential preventive measure for older adults. Incorrect Options: (A) It is a killed virus vaccine, so it is safe in immunocompromised patients Incorrect. The traditional zoster vaccine (Zostavax) is a live-attenuated virus vaccine, meaning it contains a weakened form of the virus. Live vaccines are contraindicated in immunocompromised patients, as they can cause disseminated infection. However, the newer Shingrix vaccine is a recombinant (non-live) vaccine and is safe for use in immunocompromised individuals. (B) It is not recommended for patients in this age group Incorrect. The CDC and other health authorities recommend the varicella-zoster vaccine for individuals aged 50 and older, with a strong recommendation for those over 60 to help prevent shingles and its complications. (D) It will not decrease the risk of developing shingles Incorrect. The shingles vaccine significantly reduces the risk of developing shingles. The live-attenuated vaccine (Zostavax) reduces the risk by about 50%, while the new recombinant vaccine (Shingrix) is more than 90% effective in preventing shingles.

questions.stem: All of the following respiratory viruses is a cause of the common cold syndrome in children or adults EXCEPT:
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Acute viral respiratory illnesses are the most common illness worldwide, and a wide variety of viruses have been implicated as causes. Rhinoviruses are the most common virus causing the common cold and are found in about 50% of cases. The second most commonly isolated viruses are coronaviruses. These viruses are more common in the late fall, winter, and early spring, primarily at times when rhinoviruses are less active. Other causes of common cold in children are adenoviruses, whereas these viruses are uncommon in adults with the exception of outbreaks in individuals living in close quarters such as military recruits. Although human respiratory syncytial virus characteristically causes pneumonia and bronchiolitis in young children, the virus can cause common cold and pharyngitis in adults. Parainfluenza virus is another virus classically associated with croup in children, but it causes common cold in adults. Enteroviruses most often cause an undifferentiated febrile illness.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old woman with a medical history of mild intermittent asthma presents to your clinic in February with several days of cough, fever, malaise, and myalgias. She notes that her symptoms started 3 days earlier with a headache and fatigue and that several students and teachers at her high school have been diagnosed recently with “the flu.” She did not receive a flu shot this year. Which of the following medication treatment plans is the best option for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Aspirin and a cough suppressant with codeine

options.label: B
options.text: Oseltamivir, 75 mg PO bid for 5 days

options.label: C
options.text: Rimantadine, 100 mg PO bid for 1 week

questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) The majority of influenza infections are clinically mild and self-limited. Treatment with overthe-counter cough suppressants and analgesics such as acetaminophen is often adequate. Patients who are younger than the age of 18 years are at risk of developing Reye’s syndrome if they are exposed to salicylates such as aspirin. The neuraminidase inhibitors oseltamivir and zanamivir have activity against influenza A and B. They can be used within 2 days of symptom onset and have been shown to reduce the duration of symptoms by 1 or 2 days. This patient has had symptoms for more than 48 hours, so neither drug is likely to be effective. The patient’s history of asthma is an additional contraindication to zanamivir because this drug can precipitate bronchospasm. The M2 inhibitors amantadine and rimantadine have activity against influenza A only. However, since 2005, more than 90% of A/H3N2 viral isolates demonstrated resistance to amantadine, and these drugs are no longer recommended for use in influenza A.

questions.stem: All of the following statements regarding Norwalk virus gastroenteritis are true EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: Incubation period is typically 5 to 7 days

options.label: D
options.text: It is a major cause of nonbacterial diarrhea outbreaks in the United States.

questions.answerText: Incubation period is typically 5 to 7 days
questions.solutionHtml: ation for the Correct Answer: Norwalk virus (Norovirus) is one of the leading causes of acute viral gastroenteritis worldwide. However, the statement that its incubation period is typically 5 to 7 days is incorrect. The incubation period for Norovirus is much shorter, typically 12 to 48 hours, rather than 5 to 7 days. This short incubation period contributes to the rapid spread of outbreaks, particularly in closed environments like cruise ships, schools, and nursing homes. Symptoms, including vomiting and diarrhea, usually last for 1 to 3 days and resolve without long-term complications. Explanation for Incorrect Answers: (A) Fever is common Correct statement. Although Norovirus infection is primarily characterized by vomiting, watery diarrhea, and abdominal cramps, low-grade fever is commonly observed in infected individuals. Other systemic symptoms such as headache, malaise, and myalgias can also occur. (C) Infection is common worldwide Correct statement. Norovirus is a highly infectious virus and is responsible for millions of cases of gastroenteritis globally each year. It is transmitted through the fecal-oral route, contaminated food or water, and direct person-to-person contact. Hand hygiene and proper sanitation are essential for prevention. (D) It is a major cause of nonbacterial diarrhea outbreaks in the United States Correct statement. Norovirus is one of the most common causes of viral gastroenteritis in the United States and is responsible for a significant number of foodborne illness outbreaks. It is particularly notorious for causing outbreaks in crowded settings, such as daycare centers, hospitals, cruise ships, and military barracks.

questions.stem: The human enterovirus family includes poliovirus, coxsackieviruses, enteroviruses, and echovirus. Which of the following statements regarding viral infection with one of the members of this group is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Among children infected with poliovirus, paralysis is common.

options.label: B
options.text: Enteroviruses are not transmitted via blood transfusions and insect bites.

options.label: C
options.text: In utero exposure to maternal enteroviral antibodies is not protective.

options.label: D
options.text: Infections are most common in adolescents and adults, although serious illness is most common in young children.

questions.answerText: Enteroviruses are not transmitted via blood transfusions and insect bites.
questions.solutionHtml: tion for the Correct Answer: Enteroviruses, which include poliovirus, coxsackieviruses, enteroviruses, and echoviruses, are primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route or through respiratory droplets. They are not typically transmitted via blood transfusions or insect bites, making option B correct. Enteroviruses are found in the gastrointestinal tract and can spread through contaminated water or food and close contact with an infected person. Transmission through blood transfusions and insect bites is not a recognized or common route for enteroviral infections. Explanation for Incorrect Answers: (A) Among children infected with poliovirus, paralysis is common. Incorrect. While poliovirus can cause paralysis, especially in severe cases, the majority of individuals infected with poliovirus do not develop paralysis. It is estimated that only about 0.5% to 1% of poliovirus infections lead to paralytic disease. Most infections are asymptomatic or cause mild flu-like symptoms. Thus, paralysis is not common among children infected with poliovirus. (C) In utero exposure to maternal enteroviral antibodies is not protective. Incorrect. In fact, maternal antibodies to enteroviruses, acquired during pregnancy, do provide some protection to the fetus and newborn. These antibodies can help protect the infant in the early months of life, before their own immune system is fully developed. The presence of maternal antibodies can reduce the severity or likelihood of infection, especially in the first few months after birth. (D) Infections are most common in adolescents and adults, although serious illness is most common in young children. Incorrect. Enterovirus infections are actually more common in young children, especially infants and toddlers, as they have not yet developed immunity to these viruses. While serious illness can occur in young children, including conditions like viral meningitis or myocarditis, enterovirus infections are prevalent in both children and adults. However, the severity of illness tends to be more pronounced in infants and young children, especially those with compromised immune systems.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old previously healthy female letter carrier works in a suburb in which the presence of rabid foxes and skunks has been documented. She is bitten by a bat, which then flies away. Initial examination reveals a clean break in the skin in the right upper forearm. She has no history of receiving treatment for rabies and is unsure about vaccination against tetanus. The physician should:

options.label: A
options.text: Clean the wound with a 20% soap solution.

options.label: B
options.text: Clean the wound with a 20% soap solution and administer tetanus toxoid.

options.label: C
options.text: Clean the wound with a 20% soap solution, administer tetanus toxoid, and administer human rabies immune globulin intramuscularly.

options.label: D
options.text: Clean the wound with a 20% soap solution, administer tetanus toxoid, administer human rabies immune globulin IM, and administer human diploid cell vaccine.

questions.answerText: Clean the wound with a 20% soap solution, administer tetanus toxoid, administer human rabies immune globulin IM, and administer human diploid cell vaccine.
questions.solutionHtml: ion for the Correct Answer: Rabies is a potentially fatal viral infection that is transmitted through the saliva of infected animals, typically via bites. Bats, along with foxes and skunks, are known carriers of rabies, making the potential exposure in this case concerning. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for rabies consists of a combination of rabies immune globulin (RIG) and a series of rabies vaccinations to prevent the onset of the disease after an exposure. In this case, the patient was bitten by a bat, an animal associated with rabies in the region, and has not received prior rabies vaccination. Given the risk of rabies transmission, the patient should receive human rabies immune globulin (HRIG) for immediate passive immunity, along with the human diploid cell vaccine (HDCV) for active immunity. The wound should also be thoroughly cleaned to reduce the risk of infection. Additionally, tetanus toxoid is indicated because the patient is unsure of her vaccination history and the wound was caused by an animal bite, which can introduce tetanus spores. Tetanus prophylaxis is essential for all animal bite wounds. Explanation for Incorrect Answers: (A) Clean the wound with a 20% soap solution. Incorrect. While cleaning the wound is necessary, it is insufficient by itself to address the potential rabies exposure. The patient requires both rabies immune globulin and the rabies vaccination in addition to wound cleaning. This answer overlooks the critical need for rabies PEP. (B) Clean the wound with a 20% soap solution and administer tetanus toxoid. Incorrect. This option only addresses wound care and tetanus prophylaxis, but it does not address the rabies exposure. Rabies is a life-threatening condition, and post-exposure prophylaxis (including both HRIG and the rabies vaccine) is critical after a potential exposure to rabid animals. (C) Clean the wound with a 20% soap solution, administer tetanus toxoid, and administer human rabies immune globulin intramuscularly. Incorrect. While this option includes rabies immune globulin, it does not include the rabies vaccine itself. For rabies prophylaxis, both the HRIG and the rabies vaccine are required to provide appropriate post-exposure treatment. Administering just the HRIG, without the vaccine, would be incomplete prophylaxis.

questions.stem: While working at a new medical school in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, a 35-year-old previously healthy man from Baltimore develops a sudden onset of malaise, fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, backache, and myalgias. On examination, his temperature is 39.6°C with normal blood pressure and slight tachycardia. He has some vesicular lesions on his palate and scleral injection. Laboratory studies are notable for a platelet count of 100,000/µL. All of the following are true regarding his illness EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: A second infection could result in hemorrhagic fever.

options.label: B
options.text: After resolution, he has lifelong immunity.

options.label: D
options.text: In equatorial areas, year-round transmission occurs.

questions.answerText: After resolution, he has lifelong immunity.
questions.solutionHtml: ation for the Correct Answer: The patient described is likely suffering from dengue fever, a mosquito-borne viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV). While dengue fever typically results in immunity against the infecting serotype, this immunity is not lifelong. Dengue virus has four distinct serotypes (DEN-1, DEN-2, DEN-3, DEN-4), and infection with one serotype provides immunity only against that specific serotype. Subsequent infections with a different serotype can lead to more severe forms of the disease, including hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome due to immune enhancement (antibody-dependent enhancement). Therefore, the statement that "he has lifelong immunity" is incorrect. Explanation for Incorrect Answers: (A) A second infection could result in hemorrhagic fever. Correct. A second infection with a different serotype of dengue virus can indeed lead to more severe forms of the disease, including dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF). The phenomenon is due to antibody-dependent enhancement, where pre-existing antibodies from a prior infection enhance the entry of the virus into cells, potentially leading to more severe disease. (C) IgM ELISA may be diagnostic. Correct. An IgM ELISA is often used for diagnosing dengue fever, especially early in the infection. The IgM antibodies appear in the blood within 4-5 days of infection and remain detectable for about 2-3 months, making it a useful diagnostic tool in the acute phase of the disease. (D) In equatorial areas, year-round transmission occurs. Correct. Dengue fever is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions around the world, including equatorial areas like Southeast Asia, where transmission occurs year-round due to the presence of Aedes mosquitoes (the vector for the dengue virus), which are active throughout the year in these climates. (E) The disease is transmitted by mosquitoes. Correct. Dengue virus is transmitted to humans primarily by Aedes mosquitoes, particularly Aedes aegypti. The mosquitoes become infected when they bite a person already infected with the virus, and they can then spread the virus to other individuals.

questions.stem: An ornithologist was on a 3-month trip to study severalspecies of birds living in a rain forest in SouthAmerica. On the 10th day of her trip, she was bittenon the hand by an unusually aggressive bat. The scientistapplied a topical antibiotic ointment and continuedher research. Four weeks later, the scientistlost feeling in her hand. She shortly began experiencinghigh fever, periods of rigidity, difficulty inswallowing liquids, drooling, and disorientation.Death followed rapidly. A postmortem biopsy of herbrain showed the presence of Negri bodies. Thesesymptoms are consistent with:
questions.solutionHtml: ation for the Correct Answer: The symptoms described—high fever, rigidity, difficulty swallowing liquids, drooling, disorientation, and rapid progression to death—are classic signs of rabies. The fact that the ornithologist was bitten by an unusually aggressive bat in a region where rabies is endemic strongly suggests the diagnosis. Additionally, the presence of Negri bodies on postmortem biopsy of the brain is pathognomonic for rabies infection, confirming the viral cause. Rabies is transmitted through the saliva of infected animals, and bats, especially in South America, are known to be common vectors of the disease. Explanation for Incorrect Answers: (A) California encephalitis virus. Incorrect. California encephalitis virus typically causes febrile illness, headache, and encephalitis, but it does not present with the characteristic rapid neurological decline, rigidity, difficulty swallowing, or drooling seen in rabies. The lack of Negri bodies and the presence of a bat bite further differentiate California encephalitis from rabies. (B) Hantaan virus. Incorrect. Hantaan virus causes hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which presents with symptoms such as fever, muscle aches, and kidney dysfunction, rather than the neurological symptoms described in this case. There is no association with bat bites, and Negri bodies would not be present. Hantaan virus is transmitted via rodent urine and feces, not through bat bites. (C) Ebola virus. Incorrect. Ebola virus infection can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and hemorrhagic symptoms, but it does not cause the neurological signs seen in this case, such as rigidity, difficulty swallowing, and drooling. Ebola also tends to cause more generalized hemorrhagic features, and while it can be fatal, it does not lead to the rapid onset of neurological signs seen in rabies. Furthermore, Ebola is primarily transmitted through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, not bat bites.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old female has been brought to the emergency department with complaints of mental confusion. Her parents report she had developed malaise, headache, and fever over a 2-month period, which progressed to general body pain. She does not recall any acute trauma. The patient has a history of bite by a dog with noticeable behavioral changes. On investigation the patient is found to have a high CD8+ cell count. Which agent is most likely responsible for the infection?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (D) Lyssavirus The most likely causative agent in this case is Lyssavirus, specifically the rabies virus. The patient's symptoms, including mental confusion, malaise, headache, fever, and progressive body pain, strongly suggest an evolving neurological disease. The history of a dog bite with subsequent behavioral changes is highly suggestive of rabies, a disease caused by Lyssavirus. Rabies is a zoonotic viral disease that affects the central nervous system (CNS), leading to encephalitis and ultimately death if untreated. A key feature of rabies is the presence of a strong CD8+ T cell response, which is consistent with the lab findings in this case. The virus travels retrogradely via peripheral nerves to the CNS, leading to symptoms such as agitation, hallucinations, hydrophobia, and ultimately coma. Without prompt post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), rabies is nearly always fatal. Incorrect Options: (A) Papillomavirus – This virus primarily causes skin and mucosal infections, such as warts and cervical cancer (HPV-16, HPV-18). It does not cause encephalitis, fever, or a strong CD8+ T cell response, nor is it associated with animal bites. (B) Cytomegalovirus (CMV) – CMV can cause encephalitis, but it is more commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV/AIDS or transplant recipients. CMV encephalitis does not present with a history of an animal bite or such a strong CD8+ response. (C) Coxsackievirus – This enterovirus can cause viral meningitis, encephalitis, and myositis, but it is typically associated with outbreaks in children and does not have a strong link to animal bites. Additionally, it does not typically cause the profound neurological deterioration seen in rabies.

questions.stemHtml: A 1 year old child who was born 4 weeks premature was brought to the Emergency Department with high fever, rhinorrhea, cough, and difficulty breathing. On examination, the baby had dyspnea and tachypnea; rales and wheezing were heard over both lungs. The baby was admitted to Pediatric Intensive Care where she suffered respiratory failure and was placed on mechanical ventilation. Two different types of tests for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV or Pneumovirus) were negative, as were tests for parainfluenza virus, influenza A and B viruses, and adenovirus. Which of the following viruses is the most likely etiologic agent?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) The most likely cause of this infant’s severe respiratory infection is human metapneumovirus (hMPV), a member of the Paramyxoviridae family, closely related to respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). hMPV is a major cause of acute respiratory tract infections (ARTIs) in infants, young children, and immunocompromised individuals. The child presents with fever, rhinorrhea, cough, dyspnea, and wheezing, which are hallmark symptoms of viral bronchiolitis or pneumonia. RSV is the most common cause of severe bronchiolitis in infants, but in this case, multiple tests for RSV and other common respiratory viruses were negative, making hMPV the most likely culprit. hMPV presents similarly to RSV and is often misdiagnosed due to limited routine testing availability. Premature infants are at higher risk for severe respiratory infections due to immature lung development and weaker immune defenses. hMPV typically causes upper and lower respiratory tract infections, with symptoms ranging from mild colds to severe pneumonia requiring mechanical ventilation, as seen in this case. Thus, hMPV is the best answer. Incorrect Options: (A) Cytomegalovirus (CMV) – Incorrect. CMV is a herpesvirus that can cause congenital infections and pneumonia in immunocompromised hosts, but it is not a common cause of acute respiratory failure in otherwise healthy infants. CMV pneumonia is usually chronic, affecting premature neonates and immunosuppressed individuals, such as transplant recipients. The acute presentation in this case is more suggestive of hMPV rather than CMV. (B) HSV type 1 – Incorrect. Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) can cause severe respiratory disease, but this is rare in immunocompetent children. Neonatal HSV infections usually present with encephalitis, disseminated disease, or skin/mucosal lesions, rather than isolated severe respiratory distress. Additionally, no mention of vesicular skin lesions or maternal HSV infection was provided, making HSV an unlikely cause. (D) Parvovirus B19 – Incorrect. Parvovirus B19 primarily causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) in children and aplastic crisis in individuals with hemolytic anemia. It does not typically cause severe bronchiolitis or pneumonia. Parvovirus B19 is not a common cause of acute respiratory distress in infants, making it an unlikely culprit in this scenario.

questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman working at a NGO was bitten on the fingers by a cat. She self cleaned the wounds, and after a week, the sites healed without bacterial infection. Sixty days later, she noticed pain, itching, and numbness at the sites of the bite wounds. She got scared and immediately made an appointment to see the physician next day. To physician she complained that her arm is paralyzed, and she is febrile, has a headache, and is very anxious. Doctor advice a nuchal skin biopsy. The H&E stain showed viral inclusion bodies and direct fluorescent antibody test with virus-specific antiserum was positive. With which virus was this woman infected?
questions.solutionHtml: Incorrect Options: Option A: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) CMV is a herpesvirus that typically causes asymptomatic infection or mononucleosis-like symptoms in immunocompetent individuals. It does not cause bite-related infections or progressive neurological disease like rabies. CMV encephalitis typically occurs in immunocompromised patients (HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients) and presents differently from rabies. Option B: Eastern Equine Encephalitis Virus (EEEV) EEEV is an arbovirus transmitted by mosquito bites, not animal bites. It causes encephalitis, but symptoms develop within a few days rather than weeks to months like rabies. It does not present with bite-site pain, itching, or localized neurological symptoms before progressing. Option C: Echovirus Echovirus belongs to the Picornaviridae family and is a common cause of viral meningitis and mild febrile illnesses. It is not associated with animal bites, nor does it cause progressive paralysis or Negri bodies. Unlike rabies, echovirus infections usually resolve without severe neurological complications.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician with complaints of fever, malaise, and anorexia followed by tender swelling of his parotid glands. Which of the following is the most likely complication to occur in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml: Correct Answer (C) Mumps can occasionally cause complications. Complications can include: 1. inflammation of the testicles (orchitis); this may lead to a decrease in testicular size (testicular atrophy) 2. inflammation of the ovaries (oophoritis) and/or breast tissue (mastitis) 3. inflammation in the pancreas (pancreatitis) 4. inflammation of the brain (encephalitis) 5. inflammation of the tissue covering the brain and spinal cord (meningitis) 6. deafness The most common complication of mumps virus infection in postpubertal males is orchitis, occurring in about 33% to 50% of cases. Other complications occur at lower frequencies including myocarditis meningoencephalitis, Guillain–Barré syndrome, mastitis, pneumonia, thyroiditis, pancreatitis, hearing loss, and immune thrombocytopenia purpura, which may be associated with hemorrhage. Oophoritis occurs in approximately 7% of postpubertal females.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old infant is brought to the casualty with complaints of fever, severe cough, wheezing and rapid breathing. Patient is admitted and an immunofluorescent assay is ordered which comes positive for a respiratory virus. As the infant was struggling to breathe, ribavirin treatment was started immediately. With which virus was this infant infected?
questions.solutionHtml: on of the Correct Answer: The 3-month-old infant presents with fever, severe cough, wheezing, and rapid breathing, which are characteristic symptoms of bronchiolitis. The diagnosis is confirmed by an immunofluorescent assay that detects a respiratory virus, and the patient is promptly started on ribavirin, an antiviral used in severe RSV cases. Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is the most common cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants under 6 months of age. Clinical features of RSV infection: Low-grade fever Severe cough, wheezing Tachypnea (rapid breathing) and respiratory distress Hypoxemia in severe cases Apnea in high-risk infants (e.g., premature babies, infants with congenital heart disease or chronic lung disease) Diagnosis: Confirmed by immunofluorescent assay or RT-PCR detecting RSV antigens in nasopharyngeal secretions. Treatment: Supportive care is the mainstay (oxygen, hydration, nebulized saline). Ribavirin is used in severe RSV cases in high-risk infants. Palivizumab (monoclonal antibody) is given prophylactically to high-risk infants to prevent RSV infections. Explanation of Incorrect Options: (A) Coxsackievirus A – Incorrect Coxsackievirus A is an enterovirus that does not cause bronchiolitis. It is associated with: Herpangina (fever, sore throat, vesicular lesions in the oropharynx). Hand, foot, and mouth disease (vesicular rash on hands, feet, and oral mucosa). It does not require ribavirin treatment and is not detected via immunofluorescence. (C) HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus) – Incorrect HSV primarily causes: Gingivostomatitis in young children. Neonatal herpes in newborns infected during birth. HSV pneumonia is rare and occurs in immunocompromised individuals. HSV is not a common cause of bronchiolitis in infants, and it is diagnosed using PCR or Tzanck smear, not immunofluorescence. (D) Parvovirus – Incorrect Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), which presents with: Fever and “slapped-cheek” rash in children. Aplastic anemia in patients with sickle cell disease. Hydrops fetalis in pregnant women. It does not cause respiratory distress or bronchiolitis and is not treated with ribavirin.
